exam: A 45‑year‑old man with sudden chest pain and a rapid irregular pulse presents to the ward. What is the first bedside test and what does it reveal? — ECG; shows irregular rhythm, absent P waves, wide QRS if VT.
A patient with known rheumatic mitral stenosis develops a rapid irregular pulse. Which drug is contraindicated and why? — Digoxin; risk of toxicity in hyperkalaemia and reduced renal clearance.

A 60‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with palpitations. Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely and why? — Hypokalaemia due to nephrotoxic drugs or diarrhoea, precipitating arrhythmia.

You observe a patient with a regular wide QRS complex at 140 bpm. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Ventricular tachycardia; give amiodarone or perform synchronized cardioversion if unstable.

A patient with atrial fibrillation has a normal INR but is on warfarin. What is the next step if they develop a sudden drop in blood pressure? — Suspect haemorrhage; check for bleeding, give fluids, consider reversal of warfarin.

During a ward round you note a patient with a prolonged QT interval on ECG. What is the most dangerous complication and how do you prevent it? — Torsades de pointes; correct electrolytes, stop QT‑prolonging drugs, consider magnesium.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with chest pain and tachycardia. What arrhythmia is common and what is the key investigation? — Atrial fibrillation; obtain ECG to confirm rhythm and assess for thromboembolism.
ai.title: Cardiac Electrophysiology
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Understand how the heart’s electrical system controls rhythm, recognise common arrhythmias in low‑resource settings, and apply pragmatic investigations and management while avoiding pitfalls.

b: Atrioventricular node: delay for ventricular filling
Bundle of His & Purkinje fibres: rapid conduction to ventricles
sections.p: The heart’s rhythm is generated by a coordinated electrical cascade that starts at the sinoatrial node and propagates through specialised conduction tissue.
Electrical impulses travel in a predictable sequence, producing the characteristic ECG waveform. Any disruption can alter timing or conduction velocity.

b: Heart rate variability reflects autonomic balance
Hypokalaemia shortens QT, hyperkalaemia prolongs it
sections.p: Autonomic tone modulates heart rate: sympathetic increases, parasympathetic decreases. Hormones (thyroid, catecholamines) and electrolytes (K+, Mg2+) also influence conduction.

b: Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular rhythm, loss of P waves
Ventricular tachycardia: wide QRS, rapid rate
Bradyarrhythmias: sinus node dysfunction, AV block
sections.p: Arrhythmias arise from ectopic foci, re‑entry circuits, or conduction block. In East Africa, infections (malaria, HIV), electrolyte disturbances, and rheumatic heart disease are frequent triggers.

t.b: Shows rhythm, rate, axis, QRS width, QT interval; abnormality indicates specific arrhythmia
Identify hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia that precipitate arrhythmias
Detect cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema, or infiltrates that may cause arrhythmia

b: Short‑term: treat with drugs or electrical cardioversion
sections.p: Arrhythmias can be asymptomatic or life‑threatening. Prompt recognition and treatment prevent sudden death, heart failure, or thromboembolism.

t.b: Continuous rhythm surveillance in unstable patients
Rapid bedside diagnosis when lab ECG unavailable

b: Amiodarone: broad‑spectrum antiarrhythmic, avoid in severe liver disease
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address the rhythm. Drug choice depends on stability, rhythm type, and resource availability.

t.b: Used for ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation when defibrillator not available; monitor thyroid and liver function
Control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation; avoid in hyperkalaemia

b: AV block: regular rhythm with delayed QRS, not irregular like AF
sections.p: Some conduction blocks mimic arrhythmias; distinguishing features are key.

b: Hypokalaemia may normalize QT but worsen arrhythmia risk
sections.p: Electrolyte shifts during treatment can mask or mimic arrhythmias; repeat ECG after correction.
Remember the mnemonic ‘PQRST’ for ECG components, and that a widened QRS (>120 ms) indicates ventricular origin.

whenToSeekHelp: Unstable tachycardia or bradycardia with hypotension
